identification.summary: Marigold Sandstorm is Microsoft's name for an Iran-origin actor that Microsoft previously tracked as DEV-500 (DEV-0500) [S4][S5]. MITRE ATT&CK maps Marigold Sandstorm and DEV-0500 to the group publicly known as Moses Staff (G1009) [S1]. MITRE describes Moses Staff as a suspected Iranian group that has primarily targeted Israeli companies since at least September 2021, with a stated motive of causing damage by leaking stolen data and encrypting networks without demanding a ransom [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least September 2021 [S1][S2]. Cybereason Nocturnus reported the group first spotted in October 2021 [S3][S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Marigold Sandstorm (formerly DEV-500); Microsoft's mapping file lists DEV-500 and VENGEFUL KITTEN as other names [S4]. In Microsoft's taxonomy, the Sandstorm family name denotes Iran attribution [S5]. Microsoft's mapping file does not itself list 'Moses Staff'. The Moses Staff equivalence comes from MITRE ATT&CK, which cites Microsoft's July 2023 naming page for the Marigold Sandstorm and DEV-0500 aliases [S1][S6]. MISP Galaxy groups Moses Staff, Marigold Sandstorm, DEV-0500 and VENGEFUL KITTEN as synonyms [S7].

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft classifies Marigold Sandstorm as Iran-origin [S4]. MITRE calls Moses Staff a 'suspected Iranian threat group' [S1]. No specific Iranian government organization is named in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft places the actor in its Iran (Sandstorm) family but states no confidence level in the sources gathered [S4][S5]. MITRE uses hedged language ('suspected Iranian') [S1]. Cybereason Nocturnus describes the group as an Iranian APT [S3][S7]. None of the sources gathered contains a government attribution.
attribution.basis: Microsoft's naming taxonomy and mapping [S4][S5]; Check Point Research technical analysis (November 2021) [S2] and Cybereason Nocturnus analysis (February 2022) [S3], both as summarized by MITRE ATT&CK [S1].

objectives: Politically motivated disruption and hack-and-leak against Israel: Moses Staff openly said its goal was to damage Israeli companies by leaking stolen sensitive data and encrypting victim networks, without asking for a ransom [S1][S2]. MITRE notes that DCSrv has ransomware-like functions but the group neither demands a ransom nor offers a decryption key [S1][S2]. Security researchers assess the group as politically motivated [S1][S3].

regions: Italy, India, Germany, Chile, Turkey, the UAE and the United States [S1][S3]
targeting.notes: Israeli companies are the primary focus [S1][S2]. Targeting outside Israel and the sector list come from Cybereason's February 2022 reporting as summarized by MITRE [S1][S3]. The sources gathered do not name specific victims.

capabilities.summary: Initial access through exploitation of known vulnerabilities in internet-facing infrastructure such as Microsoft Exchange servers, followed by obfuscated ASPX web shells placed under IIS paths [S1][S2]. Custom malware: PyDCrypt, a Python loader compiled with PyInstaller and tailored to each victim, which spreads across the network by opening firewall rules for SMB, NetBIOS and RPC and then drops DCSrv [S1][S2]. DCSrv is a destructive encryptor that uses the core of the open-source DiskCryptor tool and its signed drivers to encrypt whole drives. It is time-triggered and offers no ransom path [S1][S2]. The group also uses PsExec [S1][S2]. From at least November 2021 it used StrifeWater, a RAT used early in intrusions for reconnaissance, file collection, screenshots and module download, with XOR-encrypted C2 and self-deletion [S1][S3]. Data theft feeds public leaks [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Encrypt-and-leak operations against Israeli companies
campaigns.summary: Moses Staff begins attacks on Israeli organizations using PyDCrypt and DCSrv to encrypt networks and leak stolen data without demanding ransom.

campaigns.name: Check Point exposes MosesStaff ('Ideology over Money')
campaigns.summary: Check Point Research publishes the group's TTPs: Exchange exploitation, web shells, PyDCrypt/DCSrv and DiskCryptor-based encryption.

campaigns.name: StrifeWater RAT and expanded targeting
campaigns.summary: Cybereason reports the StrifeWater RAT, in use since at least November 2021, and targeting of government, finance, travel, energy, manufacturing and utility organizations outside Israel.

campaigns.name: Microsoft names the actor Marigold Sandstorm
campaigns.summary: Microsoft's threat actor naming guidance lists Marigold Sandstorm (DEV-0500), which MITRE maps to Moses Staff.

diamond.adversary: Suspected Iranian operators presenting as the Moses Staff persona; Microsoft tracks them as the Iran-origin Marigold Sandstorm [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Exchange and public-facing exploitation, obfuscated web shells, PyDCrypt, DCSrv (DiskCryptor-based full-disk encryption), StrifeWater RAT and PsExec [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Web shells on compromised IIS/Exchange servers (for example under the aspnet_client path) and StrifeWater C2 servers using XOR-encrypted traffic [S1][S2][S3]. Leak-site details are not in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Mainly Israeli companies; also government, finance, travel, energy, manufacturing and utility organizations in Italy, India, Germany, Chile, Turkey, the UAE and the US [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Anti-Israel ideology over profit: the group itself states its aim is to harm Israeli companies through leaks and encryption [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Unpatched internet-facing Microsoft Exchange servers, Windows networks reachable over SMB, RPC and NetBIOS, and abuse of signed DiskCryptor drivers [S1][S2].

gaps: Primary vendor reports could not be opened in this session: the Check Point Research report (2021-11-15), the Cybereason StrifeWater report (2022-02-01), the Fortinet 'Guard Your Drive from DriveGuard' blog and the @campuscodi tweet referenced in the actor record. Their content is cited only as MITRE ATT&CK summarizes it. The Fortinet DriveGuard reporting (newer tooling) is not reflected here.

Microsoft's own descriptive reporting on Marigold Sandstorm (as distinct from naming/mapping) was not found; the Microsoft naming page on learn.microsoft.com was unreachable. Microsoft's mapping lists DEV-500 and VENGEFUL KITTEN but not 'Moses Staff'. The Moses Staff link rests on MITRE ATT&CK and MISP Galaxy [S1][S4][S7].

MISP Galaxy records that ESET-named BiBiGun, a pro-Hamas group behind the BiBi-Linux and BiBi-Windows wipers in late 2023, showed TTP overlaps with Moses Staff [S7]. This is a separate cluster; the overlap has not been verified in primary reporting and should not be merged.

MISP Galaxy also relates Moses Staff ('likely', similar) to another cluster by UUID only. Related Iranian personas reported in the press (for example Abraham's Ax) could not be checked against sources in this session.
The specific Iranian sponsoring organization (MOIS or IRGC) and Microsoft's confidence level are not established in the sources gathered.
Activity after 2022 attributable to Marigold Sandstorm specifically, including any operations tied to the 2023-2025 Israel-Hamas or Israel-Iran conflicts, is not documented in the sources gathered.
The web search budget was exhausted during this run, so open-source coverage is incomplete. Re-run when search is available.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is internet-facing Microsoft Exchange/IIS servers and flat Windows networks where SMB and RPC can be opened between hosts [S1][S2]. Israel and partner-nation organizations in government, energy, utilities and manufacturing make up the relevant part of the environment [S1][S3]. STEP 2 (effects): Whole-disk encryption without a recovery path works as a wiper, and leaks add an information-effects layer, so impacts are both availability loss and reputational/psychological harm [S1][S2]. STEP 3 (adversary template): exploit a public-facing Exchange server, drop an obfuscated ASPX web shell, run reconnaissance (StrifeWater, whoami, domain/admin enumeration), steal data, use PyDCrypt to open firewall rules and spread with PsExec/WMIC, then time-triggered DCSrv encryption and a public leak [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is hack-and-leak plus destructive encryption against Israeli commercial and government entities timed to political events. MDCOA is the same template against partner-nation utilities or energy providers that support coalition operations, causing simultaneous outages and leaked operational data. Candidate indicators: new ASPX files under C:\inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client\system_web\, netsh firewall changes that allow SMB/RPC/NetBIOS on many hosts, DiskCryptor drivers on servers, a svchost.exe-named service outside System32, and a scheduled task impersonating the 'Firefox Default Browser Agent' [S1][S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track patch status of internet-facing Exchange/IIS assets across DODIN and mission-partner enclaves, because that has been this actor's entry point [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: encryption with no ransom path is destructive, not criminal ransomware, so an incident may need DCO response authorities and coordination on reporting a possible state-linked destructive attack. Do not treat it as extortion. (3) Mission assurance: offline backups and recovery plans for whole-disk encryption on servers supporting critical functions, and network segmentation that resists bulk firewall changes over SMB/RPC [S1][S2]. (4) Coordination: Israeli and other partner-nation victims are the primary targets [S1][S3]. Share indicators with coalition CERTs and with the DIB/critical-infrastructure partners in the sectors named, and expect leak-site publicity that may need coordination with public affairs and information operations.
